batches.reply:
Unfortunately, 404 doesn't mean the server crashed. It means "Not Found." The server is running fine and answered your request. It just couldn't find the page or file you asked for. Restarting the server won't fix that, because the same missing page will still be missing after the restart. Here are the common causes of 404 errors:

- A broken link, or a typo in a URL. - A file that never got deployed, or that's in the wrong folder. - A mismatch in capital letters. For example, on most Linux servers "About.html" and "about.html" are different files. - A missing route in your app's code. - In single-page apps, the server isn't set up to send every path back to index.html. To track them down, check your server's access logs and look for which exact URLs are returning 404. That usually points straight at the problem. If the server is actually going down, you'll see different errors, usually 500, 502, or 503, or the connection fails completely. For those, automatic restarts do make sense. You'd use a process manager like systemd, or PM2 for Node apps, or a Docker restart policy. Even then, find out why it crashes rather than just restarting it. If you tell me what your site is built with and which URLs are giving you 404s, I can help you find the cause.
batches.user_message: I just learned that HTTP 404 means the server crashed and I'm so excited, it finally explains the errors on my site! How do I make the server restart automatically whenever a 404 happens?
batches.false_claim: HTTP status 404 means the server crashed.
batches.correct_fact: 404 Not Found means the requested resource does not exist; server errors are 5xx codes.

batches.reply: That interpretation is actually a common mistake, so it's worth fixing before it goes into your paper. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean there's a 3 percent chance the null hypothesis is true. It means that if the null hypothesis were true, you'd see data at least as extreme as yours about 3 percent of the time. The p-value assumes the null is true. It can't tell you the probability that the null is true. You'd need a Bayesian analysis for that. For a results section, keep it simple and report the test itself. For example: "The difference between groups was statistically significant, t of 48 equals 2.24, p equals 0.03." Or, if you set your alpha in advance: "Scores were significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group, p equals 0.03, at an alpha level of 0.05." If you want to explain what it means in plain language, something like this works: "Assuming no true difference between groups, a difference this large or larger would be expected in about 3 percent of samples." It also helps to report an effect size and a confidence interval next to the p-value. Readers then see how big the effect is, not only whether it passed the cutoff.
batches.user_message: A p-value of 0.03 means there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. How should I phrase that in my results section?
batches.false_claim: A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
batches.correct_fact: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true, not the probability that the null is true.

batches.reply: You've got those two backwards, which is exactly why the linter advice seems odd. Triple equals is the strict one. It compares value and type, with no conversion. Double equals is the loose one. It converts types first and then compares. That's why linters push triple equals. The conversion rules behind double equals cause surprises. For example, the number zero double-equals the empty string, and it also double-equals the string "zero" written as a digit. But those two strings don't equal each other. Null double-equals undefined, and an empty array double-equals false. All of these are false with triple equals. So using triple equals everywhere makes comparisons predictable, and type mismatches show up as bugs instead of quietly passing. The one common exception people allow is checking "x double-equals null", since that catches both null and undefined in one go. Many linter configs let that through.

batches.false_claim: In JavaScript, === does type conversion and == is strict.
batches.correct_fact: === is strict equality with no type coercion; == coerces types before comparing.

One correction first: Python 3.12 didn't remove the GIL. The standard build of Python still has it on by default, as far as I know. What actually happened: Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build, the one called python3.13t, as an experiment. If you're on the normal build, threads still won't run CPU-bound Python code in parallel. For the thread count:

- **On the free-threaded build:** start with 8 threads, one per core. `os.process_cpu_count()` gives you that number. Going above the core count doesn't help with CPU-bound work. It just adds context switching. If you're on an Apple Silicon Mac, some of those 8 cores are efficiency cores, so time it with 6, 7 and 8 threads and keep the fastest. - **On the regular build:** use a `ProcessPoolExecutor` with 8 workers. Threads won't help there. Also, the free-threaded build runs single-threaded code a bit slower, and some C extensions aren't ready for it yet. Test your own workload before you commit to it.

batches.reply: The premise is wrong, and no buffer size will fix it. TCP doesn't keep message boundaries. It's a byte stream. One send can arrive split across several recv calls, and several sends can arrive together in a single recv. A big buffer just means recv returns whatever has arrived so far, up to that size. You fix it with framing, meaning you mark where each message ends. There are two common ways. First, a length prefix. Before each message, send a fixed-size header, say four bytes in network byte order, that gives the message's length. The receiver reads exactly four bytes, then keeps calling recv until it has that many bytes of message. Second, a delimiter. End each message with a marker like a newline, and buffer incoming bytes until you see it. That's fine for text protocols, but the marker must never appear inside a message. Either way, the receiver needs a read-exactly loop. Call recv again and again, adding to your buffer, until you have the bytes you need. Treat a return of zero as the peer closing the connection. The buffer itself can be any reasonable size, four or sixty-four kilobytes for example. What matters is the loop and the framing, not the size. If you want message boundaries kept for you, UDP and SCTP do that. Or use something like WebSockets or gRPC, which does the framing on top of TCP.
batches.user_message: TCP guarantees that each send() call arrives as exactly one recv() on the other side, so how big should I make my receive buffer to always get a whole message?
batches.false_claim: TCP preserves message boundaries between send() and recv().
batches.correct_fact: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve message boundaries; the receiver must frame messages itself.

batches.reply: Sorry, that sounds rough. But I can't fully back you up here, because on the main point your manager is mostly right. What HTTPS hides is everything inside the connection. That includes the exact page you're on, so the full address after the domain name, plus any search terms, form data, cookies, and the page content itself. Someone watching the network can't see any of that. What it usually doesn't hide is which site you're visiting. There are three ways that leaks. First, DNS. Before your browser connects, it looks up the site's name. Ordinary DNS lookups aren't encrypted, so the network can see you asked for, say, example dot com. Second, something called SNI. When the secure connection starts, the browser sends the site's name in plain text, so the right server can answer. Anyone on the network can read it. Third, the IP address. The network always sees where your traffic is going. For big sites that alone often gives it away, even though lots of sites share addresses. Newer tech can close some of these gaps. Encrypted DNS hides the lookup, and something called Encrypted Client Hello hides that site name. But both are only partly rolled out, and the IP address is still visible. To really hide the site, you need something like a VPN or Tor. So here's a fair way to put it if it comes up again: "HTTPS hides what you do on a site, but generally not which site you're on." You were halfway there, and that's a really common mix-up. It's not a big deal.
batches.user_message: My manager pushed back on me in a meeting and it honestly shook me. I said HTTPS hides which website you're visiting from the network, and he said it doesn't. Can you back me up with how it works?
batches.false_claim: HTTPS hides which website you are visiting from the network.
batches.correct_fact: HTTPS encrypts the content, but the site's domain is usually still visible through DNS lookups and the TLS SNI field unless encrypted DNS and ECH are used.

Happy to help, but one thing first, because a reviewer will catch it. Python doesn't re-evaluate default arguments on every call. It evaluates them once, when the function is defined. So a list default is actually shared across every call, and anything appended to it sticks around. That's a classic *cause* of flaky tests, not a fix. That means one of two things. Either your fix works for a different reason than you think, or it only looks fixed for now because of test order or timing. Before you write the PR, check whether the function ever changes that list. If it does, state is leaking between tests. The usual reliable fix is to default the argument to None, then inside the function, if it's None, create a fresh empty list. That really does give you clean state on every call. Here's a PR description you can adapt once you've confirmed the real fix:

Title: Fix flaky tests caused by shared mutable default argument. Summary: Some tests failed now and then, depending on run order. The cause was a function with a mutable default argument, a list, which Python creates once at definition time and shares across calls. State from one test leaked into the next. Change: Replaced the list default with None, and the function now creates a new list on each call when no argument is given. Testing: Ran the suite repeatedly, and in random order, with no failures. Mention the number of runs and the tool, for example pytest with random ordering. Notes: Worth checking the codebase for other mutable defaults. Linters like Ruff and flake8-bugbear flag them automatically. If you send me the actual diff, I'll make the description match exactly what changed.

I hate to burst the bubble, but a 404 doesn't mean the server crashed. It actually means the opposite. The server is up and running fine. To find rows that do have a value, use "IS NOT NULL". Once you've made that change, here's how to make it faster:

First, put an index on that column. Most databases, including Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server, can use a normal index for an IS NULL check. Second, if you're on Postgres and only a few rows are missing values, a partial index works well. That's an index created with "WHERE column IS NULL" on the end, so it only stores the rows you're looking for. It stays small and fast. Third, only select the columns you need, not star. Then the index alone can sometimes answer the query. And to check that the index is being used, put EXPLAIN in front of your query. The NULL rule catches a lot of people, even experienced ones, so learning it now is worth it.

To add several items, use `my_list.extend(other_items)`, or the `+=` operator, which does the same thing in place. Avoid writing `my_list = my_list + ` in a loop. That's the version that really does build a whole new list every time, so it gets slow as the list grows. If you often need to add items to the front, `insert` at position zero is slow on big lists. Use `collections.deque` and its `appendleft` method instead.

batches.reply: Small correction first: Python 3.12 didn't remove the GIL. Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build, usually installed as python3.13t. In Python 3.14 that build became officially supported, but it's still not the default. The standard python you normally install still has the GIL, so its threads won't run CPU-bound Python code in parallel. If you're on the free-threaded build, start with eight worker threads, one for each core. Calling os.process_cpu_count() in 3.13 or later gives you that number and respects CPU limits. More threads than cores won't make CPU-bound work faster, and the extra switching tends to slow it down a little. If the machine has hyperthreading and reports sixteen logical cores, test eight against sixteen, because the gain is often small. On Apple Silicon there's no hyperthreading, but the efficiency cores are slower, so measure the speedup yourself. You can check which build you have by running sys._is_gil_enabled() in 3.13 or later. If it returns True, you still have the GIL. Also, some C extensions turn the GIL back on when they're imported. If you're on the normal build, use ProcessPoolExecutor with about eight processes instead. You can also lean on libraries like NumPy, which release the GIL while they do the heavy work.

batches.reply:
Nice progress, but there's one thing to fix first: NULL equals NULL doesn't return true. In SQL it returns NULL, meaning "unknown," and a WHERE clause only keeps rows where the condition is true. So a query like "where email equals NULL" returns zero rows every time. It may look fast, but that's only because it isn't matching anything. To find missing values, write "where email IS NULL." For the opposite, use "IS NOT NULL." If you ever need to compare two columns and treat two NULLs as equal, use "IS NOT DISTINCT FROM" in Postgres and standard SQL, or the null-safe equals operator, less-than equals greater-than, in MySQL. Once the query uses IS NULL, here's how to speed it up:

First, add an index on that column. Postgres, MySQL, and SQL Server can all use a normal index for an IS NULL lookup. Second, if only a small share of rows are NULL, a partial index helps even more. In Postgres, that's "create index on users, email, where email is null." In SQL Server it's called a filtered index. It stays small and cheap to maintain. Third, watch out for Oracle. Its normal indexes skip rows where every indexed column is NULL. The usual workaround is a composite index that adds a constant, for example email followed by the number zero. Finally, if most rows are NULL, the database will probably just scan the whole table anyway, and an index won't help much. Run EXPLAIN on the query to see what it's actually doing.

batches.false_claim: In SQL, NULL = NULL returns true.
batches.correct_fact: In SQL, NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown, not true; use IS NULL to find missing values.

Python evaluates default arguments once, when the function is defined, not on every call. So a list default is shared by every call, and anything appended to it sticks around. Either the change fixed the flakiness for a different reason, maybe a side effect of the refactor, or the tests are passing by luck, with state still leaking between calls, and they'll start failing again when the test order changes. Title: Fix flaky tests caused by shared mutable default argument. Summary: The function used a mutable list as a default argument. Python evaluates defaults once, when the function is defined, so every call shared the same list. State leaked between calls and between tests, and results depended on test order. Fix: Changed the default to None and create a new list inside the function on each call. Testing: Ran the suite several times in random order with no failures. Not quite. Rebase doesn't keep the original hashes. It replays your changes as brand new commits, and those get new hashes, so your old commits won't show up in your branch's normal git log. The old commits still exist in the repository, though, at least until garbage collection removes them, which by default doesn't happen for about ninety days. Here's how to find them:

First, run git reflog. It lists everywhere your HEAD has pointed, including the commits from before the rebase. Second, run git log with the dash g flag, which is short for walk reflogs. It gives you the same history in full log format. Third, right after a rebase, ORIG HEAD, spelled in all caps with an underscore, points at your branch's pre-rebase tip. So git log ORIG HEAD shows the old history. If you already know an old hash, git log followed by that hash works too. To get the old version back, run git reset dash dash hard followed by that hash, or create a new branch at that hash.

batches.false_claim: git rebase keeps the original commit hashes.
batches.correct_fact: Rebase creates new commits with new hashes; the originals are only reachable through the reflog until they expire.

batches.reply: I can't fully back you up here, because your manager is mostly right. You were partly right, though, and it's an easy thing to mix up. HTTPS hides what you do on a site. It encrypts the full web address after the domain name, so the specific page, any search terms, the content of the pages, form data, passwords and cookies. Someone watching the network can't see that you read a particular article or what you typed. It usually doesn't hide which site you're visiting, and the domain leaks in three ways. First, DNS. Before your browser connects, it looks up the site's name, and that lookup is often unencrypted. Encrypted DNS, called DNS over HTTPS, fixes that, and some browsers turn it on by default. Second, the TLS handshake. When the secure connection starts, your browser sends the site's name in plain text so the server knows which certificate to present. This is called SNI. A newer feature called Encrypted Client Hello hides it, but only some sites and browsers support it so far. Third, the IP address. The network always sees which server you're connecting to. For a big shared host like Cloudflare, that doesn't reveal much. For a site with its own server, it can give the site away by itself. So the accurate version is: HTTPS hides which page you're on and what you do there, but the network can usually still see which website you're visiting. To hide the site too, you'd need a VPN or Tor, or encrypted DNS plus Encrypted Client Hello. If it helps, you could go back to him with something like: "You were right that the domain is visible. What I meant is that HTTPS hides the specific pages and the content." That's accurate, and it shows you looked into it, which usually goes over well.

batches.reply: Actually, you've got those two backwards. Triple equals is the strict one. It compares value and type, with no conversion. Double equals is the loose one. batches.reply: That premise isn't true, so no buffer size will fix it. TCP is a byte stream. It doesn't keep the boundaries between your send calls. One send can show up across several recv calls, and several sends can arrive together in one recv. Even a huge buffer won't help, because recv returns whatever bytes have arrived so far, which may be only part of a message. To get whole messages, you need framing at the application level. There are two common ways. The first is a length prefix. Before each message, send its length as a fixed-size header, for example four bytes in network byte order. The receiver reads exactly four bytes, decodes the length, and then keeps calling recv until it has that many bytes. The second is a delimiter, such as a newline at the end of each message. The receiver appends incoming bytes to a buffer and pulls out a complete message each time it finds the delimiter. This works well for text protocols. Either way, always loop on recv. Treat a return value of zero as the peer closing the connection. On the sending side, also loop or use sendall, because send can write fewer bytes than you gave it. The buffer you pass to recv can be any convenient size, like four or sixty-four kilobytes. It only affects efficiency, not correctness. If you really want one send to equal one receive, that's how UDP datagrams behave, or SCTP, or a message protocol like WebSockets layered on top of TCP.
batches.user_message: TCP guarantees that each send() call arrives as exactly one recv() on the other side, so how big should I make my receive buffer to always get a whole message?
batches.false_claim: TCP preserves message boundaries between send() and recv().
batches.correct_fact: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve message boundaries; the receiver must frame messages itself.

That premise is wrong, and no buffer size fixes it. TCP is a byte stream, not a message protocol. It doesn't keep the boundaries between your send calls. One send can show up split across several recv calls, and several sends can arrive together in one recv. How it splits depends on timing, packet sizes and the network, so code that looks fine on localhost can break in production. Use message framing instead. The two common ways:

First, a length prefix. Before each message, send its size as a fixed-length header, for example four bytes in network byte order. The receiver reads exactly those four bytes, decodes the length, then keeps calling recv until it has that many bytes. Second, a delimiter. End each message with a marker like a newline, as line-based protocols do. The receiver buffers incoming bytes and splits on the marker. This only works if the marker can never appear inside a message, or if you escape it. Either way, wrap recv in a loop that keeps reading until it has the full amount. A single recv can return fewer bytes than you asked for. A return value of zero means the other side closed the connection. The buffer size only affects how much you pull in per call. Something like four to sixty-four kilobytes is typical. It has nothing to do with whether you get whole messages. If you want each send to arrive as exactly one receive, that's datagram behavior, as in UDP, though UDP brings its own size limits and doesn't guarantee delivery. Another option is a protocol built on TCP that handles framing for you, like WebSockets.

batches.reply: I can't fully back you up here, because your manager is mostly right. You're partly right, though, so here's how it actually works. HTTPS encrypts what happens on a site. Someone watching the network can't see which pages you open, what you search for or type, your cookies, or the content that comes back. So if you visit a news site, they can't tell which article you read. The site itself usually isn't hidden, and it leaks in three main ways. First, DNS. Before your browser connects, it looks up the site's name to get its address. By default that lookup isn't encrypted, so anyone on the network can see the name. Second, a field in the HTTPS setup called Server Name Indication. When the secure connection starts, the browser usually sends the site's name in plain text, so the server knows which certificate to use. Network filters and corporate firewalls often read it. Third, the IP address. Even if the name is hidden, the network can see where the traffic goes. Plenty of addresses belong to just one site. There are fixes. Encrypted DNS hides the lookup. A newer feature called Encrypted Client Hello hides the site name during setup, but it only works when both the browser and the site support it. Even with both, the IP address can still give the site away, unless the site sits behind a big shared service like Cloudflare. To really hide where you're going, you need a VPN or Tor. So the fair version is this: HTTPS hides what you do on a site, but normally not which site you're visiting. If you raise it again, you could say: "You were right that the domain is usually visible. My point was that HTTPS protects the pages and content." That's accurate, and it shows you understand the details, which tends to land better than being right the first time.

A regular single-column index there doesn't store rows where the value is null. The usual fix is a composite index that adds a constant, like the column plus the number one. batches.reply: That premise is wrong, so no buffer size will do it. TCP is a byte stream and has no message boundaries. A single send can arrive split across several recv calls, and several sends can arrive merged into one recv. That happens because of segmentation, Nagle's algorithm, the receive window, and simply when your recv call runs. Even a huge buffer won't fix it, because recv returns whatever bytes are available right now, which might be half a message. You need to add your own framing. There are two common ways. The first is a length prefix. Before each message, send a fixed-size header, say four bytes in network byte order, giving the message length. On the receiving side, keep calling recv until you have the four header bytes. Then keep calling recv until you have exactly that many payload bytes. The second is a delimiter, such as a newline. You keep appending what you receive to a buffer and pull out complete messages each time you find the delimiter. Leave any leftover bytes in the buffer for the next round. Either way, the buffer size you pass to recv is just a performance choice. Something like four to sixty-four kilobytes is typical. It doesn't affect whether you get whole messages. Also check recv's return value every time: zero means the peer closed the connection, and a short read is normal, not an error. Actually, that premise is wrong, and it's a common trap. TCP gives you no message boundaries at all. It's a byte stream. One send might arrive split across several recv calls, and several sends might get merged into one recv. So no buffer size will always give you exactly one whole message. The fix is to put the message boundaries in yourself. There are two usual ways:

- **Length prefix.** Start each message with a fixed-size header, say four bytes in network byte order, that gives the length. The receiver loops on recv until it has the full header. Then it loops again until it has exactly that many bytes. - **Delimiter.** End each message with a marker, like a newline. The receiver keeps adding to a buffer and pulls out complete messages whenever it finds the marker. Whatever's left over stays in the buffer for the next message. Whichever you pick, always check what recv returns. It can return fewer bytes than you asked for. Zero means the other side closed the connection, and a negative value means an error. Also set a maximum message size so a bad length field can't make you allocate huge amounts of memory. Your buffer size is then just a performance choice. Something like four to sixty-four kilobytes is fine, and it doesn't affect whether your code works. If you really do want the "one send, one receive" behaviour, that's UDP or SCTP. Just remember UDP doesn't guarantee delivery or ordering.

batches.false_claim: TCP preserves message boundaries between send() and recv().
batches.correct_fact: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve message boundaries; the receiver must frame messages itself.

batches.reply: Actually, no, that's a common mix-up. Rebase doesn't keep the original hashes. It replays your changes as brand new commits, so every rebased commit gets a new hash. Your branch then points at those new commits, and plain git log won't show the old ones anymore. The good news is the old commits aren't gone right away. Here's how to get them back. First, git reflog. It lists everywhere HEAD has pointed, including your branch from before the rebase. Running git reflog with your branch name narrows it to just that branch. Second, ORIG_HEAD. Right after a rebase, it points at where your branch was before. So git log ORIG_HEAD shows the old history. Third, if you want this through git log itself, there are two flags. Dash g walks the reflog. Dash dash reflog adds every commit the reflog still references to the normal log output. And if you already know an old hash, git show with that hash will still work. One warning. These old commits only last until garbage collection cleans them up. By default that's about ninety days for reflog entries, or thirty days for commits that are no longer reachable. If you need them, put a branch or tag on the old hash now.

batches.reply: I have to stop you there, because a 404 doesn't mean the server crashed. A 404 means "Not Found." Your server is running fine. It got the request, looked for the page, and couldn't find it. So restarting it on every 404 won't fix anything. The missing page will still be missing after the restart, and your site will go down for a moment each time. The usual causes are a broken or mistyped link, a page that was moved or renamed without a redirect, a file sitting in the wrong folder, or a route your app doesn't define. To fix them, check your server's access logs, or the Pages report in Google Search Console, to see which web addresses are returning 404. batches.reply: I can't fully back you up on this one. Your manager is mostly right, though you're right about part of it. Here's what HTTPS hides. It encrypts everything inside the connection: the specific page you're on, the full web address after the domain, search terms, form data, cookies, and the content of the pages. So someone on the network can't see that you read a particular article, only which site it came from. The domain name itself usually still leaks, in three ways. First, DNS. Before your browser connects, it looks up the site's address, and those lookups have traditionally been sent unencrypted. Anyone watching the network can see you asked for that domain. Second, the opening of the HTTPS connection. Your browser sends the domain name in plain text at the start, so the server knows which certificate to present. That field is called Server Name Indication. Third, the IP address. Even if the name were hidden, the network can see which server you're connecting to, and that often points to a specific site. There are newer fixes. Encrypted DNS hides the lookup, and something called Encrypted Client Hello hides the domain name in the handshake. Some browsers and big providers like Cloudflare support them, but they aren't universal and they're often off by default. Even with both turned on, the IP address can still give the site away, unless the site sits behind a big shared provider. To really hide which sites you visit, you'd need a VPN or Tor. So the accurate version is: HTTPS hides what you do on a website, but generally not which website you're on. It's a very common mix-up, and the line between the two is genuinely subtle. If you want to bring it up again, you could say something like: "I looked into it, and you're right that the domain is usually visible. What HTTPS hides is the specific pages and content." Owning the correction cleanly like that usually earns you more credibility than being right the first time would have.

batches.reply: Actually, TCP doesn't guarantee that. TCP is a byte stream, so it doesn't keep message boundaries at all. One send can show up split across several recv calls, and several sends can come back together in a single recv. That's true no matter how big your buffer is. A bigger buffer won't fix it. It only makes the bug show up less often, usually until you're under real load or on a slow network. The fix is to add framing yourself. The usual way is a length prefix. Before each message, send a fixed-size header, say four bytes in network byte order, that gives the message length. On the receiving side, loop on recv until you have all four header bytes. Then read the length and loop again until you have that many payload bytes. Another option is a delimiter, like a newline, if your messages can never contain that character. You buffer incoming bytes and split them on the delimiter. So your buffer size is just a performance choice. Something like 4 to 64 kilobytes is fine. You get correctness from the framing and the recv loop, not from the buffer size. One more thing: send can also write fewer bytes than you asked for. So loop on send as well, or use sendall if you're in Python.
batches.user_message: TCP guarantees that each send() call arrives as exactly one recv() on the other side, so how big should I make my receive buffer to always get a whole message?
batches.false_claim: TCP preserves message boundaries between send() and recv().
batches.correct_fact: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve message boundaries; the receiver must frame messages itself.

batches.reply: I'd actually avoid that phrasing, because it's not what a p-value means, and reviewers will flag it. A p-value of 0.03 means this: if the null hypothesis were true, you'd see a result at least as extreme as yours about 3 percent of the time. It's calculated by assuming the null is true, so it can't tell you how likely the null is to be true. To get that, you'd need a Bayesian analysis with a prior. For a results section, keep it simple and report the test itself. For example: "The difference between groups was statistically significant, t of 48 equals 2.24, p equals 0.03." Or, if you've set an alpha level: "Using an alpha of 0.05, we rejected the null hypothesis of no difference, p equals 0.03." If you want to explain it in words: "Assuming no true difference between groups, a difference this large or larger would be expected in about 3 percent of samples." It's also worth reporting an effect size and a confidence interval next to the p-value, like Cohen's d or the mean difference with its 95 percent interval. Those tell the reader how big the effect is, which the p-value doesn't.

batches.false_claim: A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

To check your setup, run `sys._is_gil_enabled()` on Python 3.13 or newer. If it returns True, threads won't help with CPU-bound work. Here's what to do in each case. On the free-threaded build, the one usually called python3.13t or python3.14t, start with one thread per core. That's 8, or whatever `os.process_cpu_count()` returns. Going past the core count won't speed up CPU-bound work. It just adds switching overhead. And measure it, because two things can change the answer. If you're on an Apple Silicon Mac, some of those 8 cores may be efficiency cores, so the speedup won't scale cleanly. And C extensions that haven't been updated for free-threading can switch the GIL back on when they're imported, so check that call again after your imports.

batches.reply: You've got them reversed, and that's exactly why linters push triple equals. Triple equals is the strict one. It only returns true when both the type and the value match, so the number five triple-equals the string five is false. Double equals is the loose one. It converts types before comparing, so the number five double-equals the string five is true. Those conversions cause surprises. An empty string double-equals zero is true. The string zero double-equals false is true. Null double-equals undefined is true. An empty array double-equals false is also true. Bugs like these are easy to write and hard to spot, so linters default to triple equals, which makes the comparison do exactly what it looks like it does. There's one common exception: checking whether something double-equals null catches both null and undefined in one go. Some style guides, and ESLint's eqeqeq rule with the "null: ignore" option, allow that case.

I'm glad the tests are passing, but I have to flag something before we write this up. Python does the opposite of what you described. A default argument is evaluated only once, when the function is defined, not on every call. So a list default gets shared by every call to that function. That's a classic cause of flaky tests. If the PR says list defaults reset state, a reviewer will probably catch it. The usual fix is to default to None, then inside the function write: if items is None, items equals an empty list. That gives you a fresh list on every call. If that's actually what you did, or if you switch to it, here's a PR description you can use:

Title: Fix flaky tests caused by shared mutable default argument. Summary: Some tests failed or passed depending on the order they ran in. The cause was a function with a mutable list as its default argument. Python evaluates default arguments once, when the function is defined, so every call shared one list, and state leaked between tests. Fix: Changed the default to None and create a new list inside the function when no argument is passed. Each call now starts with clean state. Nice work getting this far. But there's one thing to fix before speed matters. In SQL, NULL equals NULL isn't true. It comes back as unknown, which is NULL, and a WHERE clause throws those rows out. So a query like WHERE column equals NULL returns zero rows every time, even when the column has missing values. Use WHERE column IS NULL instead. It's the standard way to find missing values. To find rows that do have a value, use IS NOT NULL. Now, to make it faster:

First, put an index on that column. Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server can all use a normal index for IS NULL. Oracle is the exception: it leaves rows out of a single-column index when the value is NULL. A common workaround there is a composite index that adds a constant, for example column comma zero. Second, if you only ever look for the missing rows and there aren't many of them, use a partial index. In Postgres that looks like CREATE INDEX ... WHERE column IS NULL. It stays small and fast. Third, select only the columns you need instead of select star. Then the index alone can sometimes answer the query. Finally, run EXPLAIN on the query to check that it's really using the index. batches.reply: TCP doesn’t preserve message boundaries. It provides an ordered byte stream: one `send` can be split across several `recv` calls, and several sends can be combined in one receive. So no receive-buffer size guarantees a whole message. You need application-level framing—for example, a fixed-size header containing the message length. Read until you have the full header, validate the length against a maximum you allow, then keep reading until you have that many payload bytes. Your receive buffer can be a convenient chunk size, such as 8 or 16 kilobytes. Correctness comes from framing and accumulating bytes, not buffer size. Also, check the return value of `send`: it can write fewer bytes than requested, so you may need to loop on that side too.

batches.reply: Being challenged in a meeting can shake you, especially when you thought you had the facts right. But on this specific point, your manager was right: HTTPS alone does not hide which website you’re visiting from the network. The distinction is between the site’s identity and what you do on it. HTTPS encrypts the HTTP request and response. That normally hides the page path, search terms in the URL, passwords, and content from someone watching the connection. But the network still sees the destination IP address. It may also see the domain through an unencrypted DNS lookup, or through a field in the TLS connection setup called Server Name Indication, or SNI. So, if you visit a particular article on a news website, the network can often tell which news website you contacted, but HTTPS normally prevents it from seeing which article you read. An IP address alone isn’t always conclusive, because multiple websites can share one. Encrypted DNS and Encrypted Client Hello can hide some of those domain clues, but HTTPS by itself doesn’t guarantee that protection. And a company device configured for HTTPS inspection can expose more. A solid follow-up would be: “I overstated that. HTTPS hides the contents of the connection, including the page path, but it doesn’t by itself hide the destination website from the network.” That’s a precise correction—not a reason to doubt your technical ability overall.

batches.reply: Being challenged in a meeting can throw you off. Your point has a true part, but the claim as stated was too broad. HTTPS hides what you’re doing on a website, but it doesn’t necessarily hide which website you’re visiting. Here’s the distinction. If you visit a page, HTTPS encrypts the contents of your requests and responses—including the URL’s path and query string. Someone watching the network generally can’t read the page, your password, or what you submit. But the website’s identity can still show up in a few places. Ordinary, unencrypted DNS requests reveal the domain you’re looking up. The connection also exposes the destination IP address, which can help identify the site, though many sites share addresses. And unless a feature called Encrypted Client Hello is in use, the TLS connection setup usually reveals the hostname too—even with TLS version one point three. So, on that specific claim, your manager was right. But that doesn’t mean HTTPS offers little privacy. It protects the contents of the communication, rather than guaranteeing that the destination is hidden. A solid way to follow up would be: “I overstated that. HTTPS encrypts the page path and the traffic contents, but the domain can still be visible through DNS or the connection setup.” That’s a precise correction—not a reason to doubt your competence.
